title: Control Unit Design
summary: How an opcode becomes the actual control signals that steer every mux and enable line in the datapath.

slides.markdown:
The **control unit** turns a decoded opcode into the specific set of **control signals** that steer every mux and enable line in the datapath — which ALU operation to perform, which mux input to select, whether to write the register file, whether to read/write memory.

The datapath itself is "dumb" wiring; it does whatever the control signals tell it, cycle by cycle. The control unit is the piece that actually encodes "what an instruction means" into concrete hardware behavior.

For a small instruction subset, the mapping is literally a lookup table:

![Truth table mapping opcode to control signals for a small instruction subset](assets/opcode-control-table.svg)

Each row is one instruction type; each column is one control signal. The control unit's whole job, for hardwired designs, reduces to implementing exactly this table in logic gates.

assets.alt: Truth table mapping opcode to control signals for a small instruction subset

slides.markdown:
**Hardwired control** implements the opcode-to-signals mapping directly as **combinational logic** — a fixed network of gates that computes every control signal straight from the opcode bits, with no stored program or sequencing needed.

Because it's pure combinational logic, it's fast: signals are available almost as soon as the opcode is decoded, with no extra lookup or fetch step of its own. The cost is inflexibility — changing the instruction set means redesigning the actual gate-level circuit.

**Microprogrammed control** takes a different approach: a small internal program (**microcode**) stored in a control memory *interprets* each instruction, stepping through one or more **microinstructions** that each emit one cycle's worth of control signals.

This is slower than hardwired logic (there's an extra layer of interpretation) but far more flexible: adding or fixing an instruction can mean rewriting microcode instead of redesigning silicon — which mattered enormously for CISC ISAs with large, complex instruction sets. Deep dive: [microprogramming](microprogramming).

The trade-off in one table:

| | Hardwired | Microprogrammed |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | Faster — pure combinational logic | Slower — extra interpretation layer |
| Flexibility | Low — requires new circuitry to change | High — rewrite microcode |
| Best suited to | Small, regular instruction sets (RISC) | Large, irregular instruction sets (CISC) |
| Bug/feature fixes | Silicon respin | Microcode patch (sometimes even in the field) |

Decide by asking: is the instruction set small and uniform enough to hand-design in gates, or large and irregular enough that a flexible interpreter pays for itself?

slides.sectionTitle: Why the split by ISA family
slides.markdown:
RISC's small, uniform instruction sets are exactly what hardwired control is good at — few enough instructions, and simple enough decoding, that a direct gate-level mapping stays manageable and stays fast, which matters since RISC's whole bet is on pipelining speed.

CISC's larger, more irregular instruction sets historically favored microprogramming — hand-wiring gate logic for dozens of complex variable-length instructions would have been unmanageable, while a microcode interpreter handled the complexity in a structured way, at some speed cost that CISC's other design choices could tolerate.
